memoryTip: What is common to both — a feature they share.
correctPassage: Despite cultural differences, researchers found a surprising commonality in how children learn numbers.
wrongPassages: The only commonality was that no two results shared a single pattern.
He packed a commonality in the trunk beside the spare tire.
The label commonality named a private code no other team used.

memoryTip: Animus = hostile spirit — deep dislike, not mild annoyance.
correctPassage: Years of rivalry had produced deep animosity between the neighboring towns.
wrongPassages: Their animosity showed in warm toasts and long hugs at the reunion.
The balance sheet listed animosity where a weight in grams belonged.
She felt animosity for the quiet park because it calmed her every evening.

memoryTip: Pro-fusion: pour forth in abundance — almost too much.
correctPassage: Spring brought a profusion of wildflowers to the hillside.
wrongPassages: A profusion of one spare bolt sat alone in the otherwise empty drawer.
The drought left a profusion of dry cracks and almost no living plants.
She measured the bridge’s profusion in meters and recorded 214.6.

memoryTip: Make it negative — wipe out the force of a claim or effect.
correctPassage: One contradictory finding does not negate the overall pattern in the data.
wrongPassages: New measurements negate the claim by matching it point for point.
Please negate the window before you leave so rain does not get in.
They negated the budget gap by ignoring it in every public report.

definition: understood by few; obscure or mysterious
memoryTip: Arcane knowledge sits in a secret arc — only specialists get it.
correctPassage: The paper is full of arcane terminology familiar only to specialists.
wrongPassages: The instructions were so arcane that a child finished them without help.
Her arcane welcome speech used only words every first-grader already knew.
City hall issued an arcane license that only certified the applicant’s favorite color.

memoryTip: Old golf “stymie”: your ball blocks the path — progress is stuck.
correctPassage: Missing permits continue to stymie construction on the site.
wrongPassages: Extra funding will stymie the project by clearing every remaining obstacle.
Boards postponed the stymie hire that teams had ranked first overall.
She stymied the door open so guests could walk straight in.

memoryTip: Dis-parate: not a matching pair — fundamentally different things.
correctPassage: The study brings together disparate data sources under one framework.
wrongPassages: The twins wore disparate outfits that were identical down to the buttons.
Once every source told the same story, the accounts looked fully disparate.
He stored the disparate next to packing tape in the utility closet.

definition: clear of blame; show to be right
memoryTip: Vin-dicate: clear your name — prove you were right all along.
correctPassage: Later discoveries helped vindicate scientists who had been dismissed as alarmists.
wrongPassages: New filings vindicated the suspect by adding three more charges to the case.
They hoped to vindicate the alert by auto-dismissing it the moment it fired.
She vindicated the locked file by deleting it without reading a page.

memoryTip: So shaky you pray it holds — insecure, chance-dependent.
correctPassage: The climbers’ foothold on the ridge was precarious at best.
wrongPassages: The steel beam was precarious: bolted, inspected, and rated far above the load.
Her job felt precarious after she received a permanent contract and a raise.
They called the plan precarious because every risk already had a named owner.

definition: making one feel very happy, excited, or animated
memoryTip: Ex + hilarity — thrills that leave you hilariously alive and buzzing.
correctPassage: For many students, the first research breakthrough is exhilarating.
wrongPassages: The three-hour delay on the tarmac was exhilarating for every exhausted passenger.
His exhilarating summary omitted the main result and listed only methods.
Parents described the toddler’s nap as exhilarating: calm, quiet, and brief.
